title: Scheduled Tasks
description: Make your CLI tool run itself, every day, without you opening a terminal.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what cron is and how a cron schedule expression works
Set up a cron job that runs a Node.js CLI tool on a schedule
Handle errors in a scheduled job that has no one watching it run

contentSections.body: You built a tool that summarizes your inbox every morning. Right now, it only runs when you remember to type the command. A scheduled job removes the 'remember' part entirely — it runs at 7am whether you're awake or not.

### Cron: the standard scheduler

A cron expression has 5 fields: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week.

```
*/15 * * * *   → every 15 minutes
0 7 * * *      → every day at 7:00am
0 9 * * 1-5    → 9:00am, Monday through Friday
0 0 1 * *      → midnight on the 1st of every month
```

On a machine you control, add a job with `crontab -e`:
```
0 7 * * * cd /home/you/tools/inbox-summary && /usr/local/bin/node index.mjs >> log.txt 2>&1
```

Always use full paths — cron runs with a minimal environment, and `node` on its own often won't resolve to anything.

contentSections.question: Your cron job works fine when you run the command manually, but silently does nothing when cron triggers it. What's the most likely cause?
contentSections.answer: **Cron runs with a different, minimal environment than your interactive shell.** Environment variables like `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and even `PATH` may not be set the way they are in your terminal. The fix: use full paths to binaries, and explicitly load environment variables (e.g. via a `.env` file loaded with dotenv, or sourcing them at the top of the crontab entry).
contentSections.hint: What's different between typing a command yourself and cron typing it for you?

contentSections.body: Cron runs in a minimal environment. Use full paths and load your environment variables explicitly — don't assume anything from your interactive shell carries over.

**Log successes too, not just failures.** A job that stopped running entirely (cron itself broken, machine off) produces no error — just silence. A daily 'ran successfully' log line lets you notice the gap when you check back.

title: Webhooks
description: React to something happening, instead of checking on a schedule whether it happened.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the difference between polling and webhooks
Build a webhook endpoint that receives and processes an event
Verify a webhook's signature to confirm it's genuine

contentSections.body: A scheduled job that checks every 5 minutes whether a new order came in is polling — asking the same question over and over, mostly getting 'no.' A webhook flips that: the order system calls your tool the instant an order happens. No waiting, no wasted checks.

contentSections.question: Why does the webhook handler above respond `res.status(200).send('OK')` immediately, even before `summarizeAndNotify` fully finishes in a real production setup?
contentSections.answer: **Most webhook senders expect a fast response and will retry (or give up) if you're slow.** In production, best practice is to acknowledge receipt immediately, then process the actual work — often by queuing it — separately. A webhook handler that takes 10 seconds to respond risks the sender timing out and resending the same event, causing duplicate processing.
contentSections.hint: What happens if a webhook sender doesn't get a response within a few seconds?

contentSections.body: Webhooks push events to you instead of you polling for them. Acknowledge receipt fast; do slow work separately.

**An unverified webhook endpoint is an open door.** Without signature verification, anyone who guesses or finds your URL can trigger your tool with fake data — including fake payment confirmations or fake events that cause real actions in your system.

title: Sending Results to Slack
description: Your tool's output, posted where your team already looks — instead of sitting in a terminal.

learningObjectives.text: Set up a Slack incoming webhook for a workspace channel
Post formatted messages to Slack from a Node.js script
Format tool output using Slack's block/markdown formatting

contentSections.title: A URL that posts to a channel

contentSections.body: You've built a tool that flags concerning patterns in customer feedback. Right now the output is a JSON file nobody opens. Post it to a Slack channel instead, and it's read within minutes instead of never.

contentSections.question: Where should the Slack webhook URL live in your code — hardcoded in the script, or in an environment variable?
contentSections.answer: **An environment variable.** A Slack webhook URL is a secret — anyone with it can post messages into that channel as your integration. It follows the same rule as an API key: never hardcoded, never committed, loaded from `.env` or your deployment platform's secret storage.
contentSections.hint: What could someone do if they got hold of that URL?

contentSections.body: A Slack incoming webhook URL is a secret, not a config value — treat it like an API key.

**Keep automated Slack messages short and skimmable.** A message someone has to scroll to read gets ignored after the first few days. If the full detail matters, post a short summary with a link to the full output somewhere else.

title: Sending Results by Email
description: Deliver your tool's output to an inbox, for the people who don't live in Slack.

learningObjectives.text: Send a transactional email from a Node.js script using an email API
Format an email with both plain text and HTML versions

contentSections.title: Why an email API instead of raw SMTP

contentSections.body: You could configure raw SMTP to send email from your script. You could also spend an afternoon fighting spam filters, SPF records, and DKIM signing. An email API like Resend handles all of that — you send one HTTP request, they handle deliverability.

contentSections.question: Why include both a `text` and an `html` version of the same email, instead of just sending HTML?
contentSections.answer: **Not every email client renders HTML the same way, and some spam filters weight plain-text-only emails as more trustworthy when a text fallback exists.** Including both is the accepted standard for transactional email — the recipient's client picks whichever it can render best, and you're covered either way.
contentSections.hint: Think about accessibility tools and older or minimal email clients too.

contentSections.body: Always send a plain-text fallback alongside HTML. It's a deliverability and accessibility standard, not an optional extra.

**Don't retry immediately and repeatedly on a hard failure.** An invalid email address will fail every retry identically — back off with increasing delays, and give up after a small number of attempts rather than hammering the API.

title: Chaining Automations
description: One tool's output becomes another tool's trigger. Build a small automated pipeline.

learningObjectives.text: Design a multi-step automation where each tool's output triggers the next step
Identify failure points in a chained automation and add appropriate error handling
Build a complete scheduled pipeline combining a Claude call, a decision, and a delivery step

contentSections.body: Each tool you've built so far does one thing: summarize, notify, schedule. A pipeline chains them — a scheduled job pulls data, Claude analyzes it, a decision routes the result, and delivery sends it to the right place. That's most of what 'automation' means in practice.

contentSections.question: In the pipeline above, if the Slack post for an urgent item fails (network error), should the whole pipeline stop, or should it continue processing the remaining entries?
contentSections.answer: **It should continue, and log the failure separately.** One failed delivery shouldn't block every other entry from being processed — a single network blip taking down an entire day's triage is a worse outcome than one missed Slack notification that gets logged and can be manually checked. Wrap each delivery step in its own try/catch, not the whole loop.
contentSections.hint: What's the cost of one failed step vs. the cost of the whole pipeline halting?

contentSections.body: In a chained pipeline, isolate failures to the step where they happen. One broken delivery shouldn't take down everything after it.

contentSections.title: Designing for the failure you can't predict

contentSections.body:
Every chained automation has more failure points than a single tool. Before shipping one, walk through each step and ask what happens if it fails:

```
Step                          If it fails...
────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────
Fetch feedback from DB        Log error, skip this run, alert — nothing to process is fine
Claude classification         Retry once; if still failing, default to 'normal' (safe default,
                               human reviews it in the digest rather than losing it silently)
Slack post (urgent)           Log + fall back to including it in the email digest too
Email digest send             Retry with backoff; if it still fails, save digest to a file
                               so nothing is lost even if delivery is broken
```

The pattern across all of these: prefer a degraded but visible outcome (item shows up late, or in the wrong channel) over a silent loss (item disappears entirely). A pipeline you don't watch every day needs to fail safely on its own.

**Build the pipeline as separate, individually-testable functions**, exactly like the mocking pattern from the testing module — `fetchNewFeedback`, `classify`, `postToSlack`, `sendSummaryEmail` — then compose them in `runTriagePipeline`. Each piece stays testable on its own, and you can debug a broken pipeline by testing one link at a time.
